claim: Visual perception and behavior are mediated by cortical areas that have been distinguished using architectonic and retinotopic criteria.
source: Visual perception and behavior are mediated by cortical areas that have been distinguished using architectonic and retinotopic criteria.
evidence: This is a general statement about visual cortex organization supported by established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Fluorescence imaging and GCaMP6 reporter mice were employed to generate retinotopic maps.
source: We employed fluorescence imaging and GCaMP6 reporter mice to generate retinotopic maps, revealing additional regions of retinotopic organization that extend into barrel and retrosplenial cortices.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used in the study.

claim: Additional regions of retinotopic organization extend into barrel and retrosplenial cortices.
source: We employed fluorescence imaging and GCaMP6 reporter mice to generate retinotopic maps, revealing additional regions of retinotopic organization that extend into barrel and retrosplenial cortices.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: There is a mismatch in border location between retinotopic maps and architectonic borders.
source: Aligning retinotopic maps to architectonic borders, we found a mismatch in border location, indicating that architectonic borders are not aligned with the retinotopic transition at the vertical meridian.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data comparing different mapping approaches.

claim: Architectonic borders are not aligned with the retinotopic transition at the vertical meridian.
source: Aligning retinotopic maps to architectonic borders, we found a mismatch in border location, indicating that architectonic borders are not aligned with the retinotopic transition at the vertical meridian.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed mismatch between border locations.

claim: Four visual areas bordering V1 (LM, P, PM and RL) display complementary representations.
source: We also assessed the representation of visual space within each region, finding that four visual areas bordering V1 (LM, P, PM and RL) display complementary representations, with overlap primarily at the central hemifield.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of visual field coverage in different areas.

claim: The four visual areas bordering V1 have overlap primarily at the central hemifield.
source: We also assessed the representation of visual space within each region, finding that four visual areas bordering V1 (LM, P, PM and RL) display complementary representations, with overlap primarily at the central hemifield.
evidence: This describes the pattern of overlap observed in the visual field coverage analysis.

claim: Mouse cortex contains up to 16 distinct retinotopically organized regions.
source: Our results extend our understanding of the organization of mouse cortex to include up to 16 distinct retinotopically organized regions.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the mapping results presented in the study.

claim: In mouse neocortex, 12 visual areas have been identified, each corresponding to a retinotopically-organized map of the visual field.
source: In mouse neocortex, 12 visual areas have been identified, each corresponding to a retinotopically-organized map of the visual field (Dräger, 1975; Wagor et al., 1980; Olavarria et al., 1982; Olavarria and Montero, 1989; Schuett et al., 2002; Kalatsky and Stryker, 2003; Wang and Burkhalter, 2007; Marshel et al., 2011; Wang and Burkhalter, 2013; Garrett et al., 2014; Tohmi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Architectonic borders are associated with changes in staining (chemoarchitectonics), cell density (cytoarchitectonics), or myelination patterns (myeloarchitechtonics).
source: Architectonic borders are associated with changes in staining (chemoarchitectonics), cell density (cytoarchitectonics), or myelination patterns (myeloarchitechtonics).
evidence: This is a definition based on established knowledge in neuroanatomy.

claim: Retinotopic borders are associated with a change in chirality of the retinotopic map.
source: Retinotopic borders are associated with a change in chirality of the retinotopic map and have been identified anatomically by labeling projections between visual areas, and functionally by recording the responses of neurons with electrodes or imaging techniques.
evidence: This is a definition based on established knowledge in visual neuroscience.

claim: The architectonic and retinotopic borders of visual areas in the mouse are generally thought to be co-aligned.
source: The architectonic and retinotopic borders of visual areas in the mouse are generally thought to be co-aligned, but the shapes and locations of visual areas can differ across studies.
evidence: This describes the prevailing assumption in the field prior to this study.

claim: The shapes and locations of visual areas can differ across studies.

claim: Retinotopic maps were generated from GCaMP6 transgenic mice.
source: We generated retinotopic maps from GCaMP6 transgenic mice (Chen et al., 2013; Madisen et al., 2015) and compared functional retinotopic, anatomical retinotopic, chemoarchitectonic, cytoarchitectonic and myeloarchitechtonic maps.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach with citation to the mouse lines used.

claim: Functional retinotopic, anatomical retinotopic, chemoarchitectonic, cytoarchitectonic and myeloarchitechtonic maps were compared.

evidence: This describes the comparative analysis performed in the study.

claim: The results revealed new regions of retinotopic organization in mouse neocortex.
source: Our results revealed new regions of retinotopic organization in mouse neocortex, some within and some outside the accepted boundaries of mouse visual cortex, and a mismatch between retinotopic and architectonic maps that may help reconcile the differences between visual area maps generated by these complementary approaches.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study.

claim: Some new regions of retinotopic organization are within the accepted boundaries of mouse visual cortex.

claim: A spherically-corrected checkerboard visual stimulus drifting across the visual field at 0.043–0.048 Hz was employed to generate retinotopic maps.
source: To generate retinotopic maps, we employed a spherically-corrected checkerboard visual stimulus drifting across the visual field at 0.043–0.048 Hz (Figure 2A) (Kalatsky and Stryker, 2003; Marshel et al., 2011) and mapped retinotopy in Emx1-GCaMP6 mice that were head-restrained and free to run on a rotating disk.
evidence: This describes the visual stimulus used for mapping, with citations to prior methods.

claim: Retinotopy was mapped in Emx1-GCaMP6 mice that were head-restrained and free to run on a rotating disk.
source: To generate retinotopic maps, we employed a spherically-corrected checkerboard visual stimulus drifting across the visual field at 0.043–0.048 Hz (Figure 2A) (Kalatsky and Stryker, 2003; Marshel et al., 2011) and mapped retinotopy in Emx1-GCaMP6 mice that were head-restrained and free to run on a rotating disk.
evidence: This describes the experimental setup for awake imaging.

claim: The mean fluorescence change was greatest in visual cortex.

evidence: This is an observation from the imaging data.

claim: 10–40 presentations of the stimulus in each of the four cardinal directions were averaged to generate retinotopic maps.
source: To generate retinotopic maps, we averaged 10–40 presentations of the stimulus in each of the four cardinal directions, thereby reducing the potential effects of ongoing activity (Figure 2D; Video 1).
evidence: This describes the data averaging procedure used in the analysis.

claim: Averaging 10–40 presentations of the stimulus reduces the potential effects of ongoing activity.

evidence: This describes the range of visual space covered by the maps.

claim: Mean eye displacement was <~1 degree.

claim: A stimulus with constant mean luminance was employed to minimize systematic changes in pupil size.
source: To minimize systematic changes in pupil size, we employed a stimulus with a constant mean luminance, delivering the moving checkerboard pattern on a grey background with 50% of the maximum luminance (Figure 2—figure supplement 5, Videos 2,3).
evidence: This describes a design choice to control for potential confounds.

claim: Maps were largely unaffected by eye movements or changes in pupil size.
source: Hence, in our experiments maps were largely unaffected by eye movements or changes in pupil size.

claim: Twelve discrete areas have been identified in mouse visual cortex.
source: Twelve discrete areas have been identified in mouse visual cortex: primary visual cortex (V1), lateromedial area (LM), rostrolateral area (RL), anterior area (A), anteromedial area (AM), posteromedial area (PM), medial area (M), posterior area (P), postrhinal area (POR), laterointermediate area (LI), anterolateral area (AL), and laterolateral anterior area (LLA) (Dräger, 1975; Wagor et al., 1980; Olavarria et al., 1982; Olavarria and Montero, 1989; Wang and Burkhalter, 2007; Garrett et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a summary of prior literature on mouse visual areas.

claim: Each visual area contains one retinotopic map.
source: Each area contains one retinotopic map and therefore appears in field sign maps as a single, distinct, positive or negative field sign patch (Sereno et al., 1994, 1995).
evidence: This is a definition based on established knowledge with citations.

claim: Each visual area appears in field sign maps as a single, distinct, positive or negative field sign patch.
source: Each area contains one retinotopic map and therefore appears in field sign maps as a single, distinct, positive or negative field sign patch (Sereno et al., 1994, 1995).
evidence: This is a consequence of the definition of visual areas with citation to prior work.

source: Across mice these patches are arranged in a stereotyped configuration with consistent positioning relative to each other.

claim: An automated image analysis approach was used to identify field sign patches that each contain one and only one map of retinotopic space.
source: To identify regions in our maps objectively, we used the automated image analysis approach described by Garrett et al. (2014), which identifies field sign patches that each contain one and only one map of retinotopic space.
evidence: This describes the analysis method with citation to prior work.

claim: Most field sign patches were visible after only 15 min of imaging.
source: Most field sign patches were visible after only 15 min of imaging (Figure 3A; 10 sweeps of the stimulus in each direction) and maps were stable across imaging sessions (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an observation about the efficiency of the GCaMP6-based mapping approach.

claim: Maps were stable across imaging sessions.
source: Most field sign patches were visible after only 15 min of imaging (Figure 3A; 10 sweeps of the stimulus in each direction) and maps were stable across imaging sessions (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an observation about the reproducibility of the maps.

source: The ability to quickly generate maps that are comparable to those resulting from 1–2 hr of red-wavelength reflectance-based imaging under anesthesia (Garrett et al., 2014) is a practical advantage of GCaMP6 fluorescence-based mapping.

claim: Maps displayed consistent structure across mice.
